summary: Describes properties of and relationships among Real-time Transport Protocol sources, both existing and proposed, and defines common terminology for discussing them, since the terms can be complex and confusing.

plainLanguage.summary: This RFC gives a shared vocabulary for how audio and video move through RTP systems. It explains how streams, sessions, participants, and media-processing steps relate.

questions: what is the terminology for rtp sources
what is the difference between an rtp stream and an rtp session
what do srst and mrmt mean
subtitle: A common vocabulary for RTP streams, media sources, sessions, and participants.

tldr.problem: RTP terminology can be confusing because different specifications use the same words differently and hide complexity between layers.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC describes a media chain of streams and transformations, defines communication entities, and explains relationships among RTP sources.
tldr.outcome: This Informational RFC clarifies terminology; it does not define a new protocol or add security considerations beyond RTP and the protocols using it.

today: RFC 7656 is an Informational terminology document published in November 2015. The batch metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why RTP Terms Need a Taxonomy
sections.content:
The RFC says that terminology about RTP sources and their relationships has been considered confusing and inconsistent. Protocols that use RTP may use the same term for different things, and one layer may hide complexity handled elsewhere.

It organizes the topic by describing media transformations between sender and receiver, the entities involved in communication, and how streams can be grouped or associated.
sections.plainLanguage: Different RTP documents can use familiar terms in different ways. This RFC gives readers a shared set of definitions for discussing RTP media.

sections.title: The Sender and Receiver Media Chain
sections.content:
The RFC models media as time-based streams that pass through transformations. On the sender side, capture can produce raw media, a source produces a clock-synchronized stream, an encoder creates an encoded stream, and a packetizer creates RTP packets. Redundancy and security transformations may also be used.

The receiver reverses these steps through validation, repair, depacketizing, decoding, and rendering. The received streams may differ from those sent because of lossy encoding or packet loss that repair cannot fix.
sections.plainLanguage: A sender captures and encodes media, then packs it into RTP packets. The receiver checks and unpacks the packets, but loss or encoding can make the received media differ from the original.

sections.title: Streams, Sessions, and Participants
sections.content:
An RTP stream is a sequence of RTP packets identified by an SSRC within an RTP session. An RTP session is a group communication channel that can carry multiple streams and shares an SSRC space and RTCP bandwidth.

An endpoint sends or receives RTP packets. A participant is an entity reachable through a signaling address, and a multimedia session connects participants through one or more RTP sessions. A communication session associates participants through one or more multimedia sessions.
sections.plainLanguage: An RTP stream is one identified flow of media packets. An RTP session can carry several streams, while participants and multimedia sessions describe the larger communication.

sections.title: How Related Streams Are Organized
sections.content:
The RFC defines a synchronization context as a requirement for a strong timing relationship between media sources. It describes simulcast, where one source becomes several independent encoded streams, and layered multi-stream, where parts of a scalable encoding use separate RTP streams.

For layered multi-stream, SRST means one RTP stream on one media transport, MRST means multiple RTP streams on one media transport, and MRMT means multiple RTP streams on multiple media transports. Stream duplication, retransmission, and forward error correction are also described as ways to provide redundancy.
sections.plainLanguage: A media source can be sent in several versions or protected with extra data for recovery. The receiver needs identifiers and relationships to know how those streams fit together.

sections.title: Mapping Terms from Other Specifications
sections.content:
The RFC maps selected terms from telepresence, WebRTC, and other specifications to the concepts in its taxonomy. For example, a WebRTC RtcMediaStream groups media sources that share a synchronization context, and an RtcMediaStreamTrack describes a media source.

It also explains that terms such as Multi-Session Transmission can be ambiguous. The taxonomy maps that term to multiple streams on one or more media transports, depending on the arrangement.
sections.plainLanguage: This section translates terms used by other specifications into the shared vocabulary. It also points out where an existing term can mean more than one thing.

items.title: SRST
items.text: One RTP stream on one media transport.

items.title: MRST
items.text: Multiple RTP streams on one media transport.

items.title: MRMT
items.text: Multiple RTP streams on multiple media transports.
